title: When Tech Is a Tool, Not a Crutch
author: Tara Laskowski
summary: In this Educational Leadership interview, editorial director Tara Laskowski asks two University of Michigan undergraduates, Masson Sam and Johan Houdebine, what they learned about AI, attention and digital balance that they wish their teachers had taught them. Both were in high school when ChatGPT arrived and describe teachers who simply banned it, leaving students to figure out responsible use on their own. In college they found AI encouraged, used it to build a startup demo and speed routine work, and came to see AI fluency as essential for their careers. Their advice to K-12 teachers is to treat AI as a monitored classroom tool with an explicit ethical framework rather than an outlawed shortcut. They also describe personal habits for staying digitally healthy in an attention economy, such as avoiding the phone for the first hour of the day.
points: The students say the high school message was simply do not use it, with no framework for ethical or effective use.
Houdebine used ChatGPT as a tutor, for example generating extra calculus practice problems, while keeping final decisions for himself.
They recommend keeping AI inside the classroom where teachers can monitor it, especially for younger students.
Sam worries that unequal access to AI will widen gaps in capability between communities.
quotes: Without clear guidelines from their teachers or school leaders on how to use such a transformative technology, they and their classmates were left to figure it out for themselves.

I saw ChatGPT as a tool that could help me, but I still had to retain my autonomy as a person. I couldn’t let it make the final decision. I approached it with that type of mindset and used it more like a tutor.
Sam: Yeah, there was no framework, and I think we needed some level of encouragement to learn how to use these tools ethically and understand their capabilities.
Houdebine: Treat AI as a tool, but keep it within the classroom so you can monitor its use—especially for younger students.
Houdebine: Try learning about using AI in a responsible way that extends your learning, not replaces it, and see what you can create.

Sam: We’re in an attention economy. These giant social media companies’ algorithms are designed to keep you on their apps as long as possible. So for me, being intentional with my use of technology is important.

When I wake up, I try my best not to touch my phone or look at emails at all for the first hour. And the benefit of that is starting the day with clarity and not having to worry about anything else other than that present moment.
